transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Hi, Dr. Smith. Well, I'm here because... we recently put a new, brighter mirror in our bathroom at home, and ever since then, I just keep noticing my face. 

Specifically, the skin around my cheeks and my jaw. It just looks really uneven to me, or kind of saggy. I've pointed it out to my husband, but he says he can't really see what I'm talking about. But I just keep seeing it, and it's really been bothering me.
About how many hours a day would you say you spend thinking about or checking on your skin's appearance?

I'd say maybe an hour or so total, if you add it all up throughout the day. Most mornings I end up checking my face from a few different angles in that mirror, and I'll usually put on a little extra makeup before I leave for the courthouse. 

During the day, I don't constantly stare in a mirror, but... sometimes I do catch myself comparing my face to the other women I see at work. And if someone wants to take a casual picture and I’m not feeling okay about how my skin looks, I usually just try to avoid being in it.

latest_inference.note: Patient's focus is specifically on perceived skin/facial flaws not noticed by others, with checking, camouflaging (extra makeup), and avoidance (skipping photos) behaviors—classic for BDD. No evidence of pervasive attention-seeking or emotional lability (ruling out F60.4) or generalized, diffuse worry beyond appearance (ruling out F41.1).

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance (uneven/saggy facial skin) that is not observable or appears slight to others (husband cannot see what she describes), leading to repetitive behaviors including mirror checking, camouflaging with makeup, comparing her appearance to others, and avoidance of photographs. Preoccupation occupies about an hour daily, meeting time criterion for BDD. She retains insight into the exaggerated nature of her concern (acknowledges husband cannot see the flaw, framing it as her own perception), ruling out a delusional disorder (F22) or psychotic-level BDD. No other psychotic symptoms, mood disturbance, or eating disorder features reported that would better explain the symptoms.
